description:
Hi! I’m Saadan Khokhar, a space enthusiast from Pakistan who loves exploring big ideas and turning them into real, working projects. I enjoy problem-solving, research, and building things quickly.

Why join us?
We’re all about shipping. Our plan is simple: pick one clear problem, use real NASA data, and build a working prototype with a polished demo by the deadline.
summary: Escape Velocity: Mission Architect is a free browser game where players design, launch and fly a complete space mission, from first idea to final science report. Players choose a mission (Earth observation, Mars, an infrared telescope at L2, a low-cost lunar CubeSat, or a free sandbox). Then they choose an orbit, rocket, spacecraft, instruments and communications, while a live dashboard tracks mass, power, budget, data, Δv and lifetime. Every choice has consequences, and there's no single right answer. Up to four players can share the work as Mission Director, Spacecraft Engineer, Science Lead and Operations Lead, each with a priority that conflicts with the others, so the team has to negotiate. A month-by-month simulation with random events ends in a scored report that explains why the mission succeeded or failed and compares the design with a real NASA mission. Abstract systems-engineering trade-offs become hands-on decisions anyone can try in minutes.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Escape Velocity: Mission Architect lets students and space fans work through the whole mission design process that real teams follow. The steps follow NASA JPL's Concept Maturity Levels: CML 1 Mission Idea, CML 2 Feasibility (orbit and launch), CML 3 Trade Studies (spacecraft, instruments, comms and ground), and CML 4 Point Design (a Go/No-Go design review). After the review, the player launches the mission and watches it fly.

HOW IT WORKS

• 5 scenarios: Earth Watch (wildfire and crop monitoring from low Earth orbit), Red Planet Recon (mapping buried ice on Mars), Deep Sky Eye (an infrared observatory), Lunar Pathfinder (a CubeSat on a $60M budget), and a Sandbox where players write their own objective.

• Real trade-offs: 5 orbits, 5 launch vehicles, 4 spacecraft sizes, plus solar arrays, an RTG, batteries, onboard computers, attitude control, propulsion, redundancy, 12 instruments, 4 radios, a high-gain dish and 3 ground networks. Every part has mass, power and cost. Instruments also produce data and need a certain pointing accuracy. A bigger camera means more science, but also more mass, power, cost and data to downlink.

• Live dashboard: colored bars for launch mass vs rocket capacity, payload, power, battery, budget, data vs downlink, Δv, lifetime and estimated science, plus a spacecraft drawing that redraws as parts are added.

• Realistic checks: the rocket must be able to lift the spacecraft to the chosen orbit, the propulsion must provide enough Δv to enter that orbit, the batteries must survive eclipses, and the mission must stay within budget. Every failed check comes with a plain-English fix hint.

• Team mode for up to 4 players: each role owns part of the design and has a priority that pulls against the others (under budget vs high science vs safety margins vs data downlink). Negotiation alerts show the numbers behind each conflict, and every player must vote GO before launch.

• Simulation: an animated launch, transfer and operations phase, with live meters for battery, power, data storage, propellant and science. Month-by-month random events include solar storms, reaction wheel failures, micrometeoroid hits, ground antenna faults and unexpected discoveries.

• Mission report: a score out of 1000 across science, objectives, budget, engineering margins and team priorities, plus a grade. It explains what went well and what to improve using the actual numbers, names who would use the mission's data, and compares the design with a real mission (Landsat 9, NISAR, Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, JWST, CAPSTONE, LunaH-Map).

• Replay and share: Redesign & Fly Again, a "Compare attempts" table, a leaderboard filtered by scenario and difficulty, and design codes that can be exported and imported so teams can challenge each other.

• Accessible to beginners: a first-visit tutorial, "Learn" boxes on every step, three difficulty levels (Cadet hides advanced parts), and an About & Sources panel linking to NASA resources.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Students rarely get to experiment with a whole mission. This game makes the system-level lesson concrete: improving one thing costs something somewhere else, and several different designs can all succeed. Players learn from both successful and failed missions, and the report explains the cause instead of just marking a choice right or wrong. It runs in any browser, on a laptop or a phone, with no installation and no account, so a classroom can use it right away.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

Team roles have deliberately conflicting priorities, so players have to negotiate like a real mission team. A Go/No-Go flight readiness poll and design codes let teams compete on the same objective.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript in a single file, using Canvas for the simulation and SVG for the spacecraft preview, hosted on GitHub Pages. It was tested with Node.js unit checks and 99 automated headless-browser tests (Playwright) covering all scenarios, team sizes, difficulties and phone screens. Developed with SI assistance (Anthropic Claude), as disclosed in the project. The mission model is deliberately simplified for learning: its numbers are illustrative but inspired by real missions and NASA mission design resources.

FUTURE PLANS

More scenarios (asteroid sample return, outer-planet missions), online multiplayer so teams can play from different devices, more realistic trajectories based on NASA's GMAT, a classroom mode for teachers, and translations, starting with Urdu.

Source code: https://github.com/SaaKho/escape-velocity-mission-architect
